```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import great_docs as gd

gd.enable_tbl_preview(n_head=8, n_tail=3)
```

A static drawing is the right choice for a report, but exploring a network is a different activity.
It calls for dragging a crowded region apart, zooming in on a cluster, and clicking a node to see
what it is. EdgeCase has several interactive views for this, each built on a different rendering
technology and suited to a different size of graph:

| View | Built on | Interaction | Suits |
|---|---|---|---|
| `plot()` | SVG | hover tooltips | reports, documents, any size up to a few thousand edges |
| `plot_vis()` | vis-network | live physics, dragging, zooming, a click panel | hands-on exploration of small and medium graphs |
| [`graph_widget()`](../reference/graph_widget.qmd) | HTML canvas | dragging, panning, zooming, hover tooltips | notebook exploration with colors and sizes from the data |
| `plot_cosmo()` | Cosmograph (WebGL) | GPU layout, zooming, selection | graphs of many thousands of nodes and more |
| step players | SVG and JavaScript | stepping through recorded operations | teaching and explaining algorithms |

All of them run in the browser, so they work in Jupyter notebooks, in VS Code, and in rendered
documents, and most of them can also be saved as standalone HTML files to share. This page
describes each view in turn.

## Tooltips in static plots

The drawings made by `plot()`, described in [Static plots](plotting.qmd), are already
interactive in a modest way. When they are displayed in a notebook or a web page, hovering over a
node shows a tooltip with its ID and attributes, and hovering over an edge shows the edge's
attributes. Any attribute stored on the graph appears, including the results of analysis methods:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec
import polars as pl

karate = ec.karate_club()
karate.pagerank()
karate.plot(color_by="faction", size_by="pagerank", label_by="label", seed=1)
```

Hovering over the large node `"33"` shows its node ID, 34, that it belongs to faction 2, that its
role is Administrator, and that it has the highest PageRank of the club. The tooltips make it
possible to leave most nodes unlabelled and still identify any node of interest. They need
JavaScript, so they are kept when a plot is saved with a path ending in `.html` and lost when it is
saved as plain SVG:

```{python}
#| eval: false
karate.plot(color_by="faction", size_by="pagerank", seed=1, output="karate.html")
```

## Live physics with plot_vis()

`plot_vis()` draws the graph with [vis-network](https://visjs.github.io/vis-network/), a
JavaScript library for interactive network diagrams. The library is bundled with EdgeCase, so the
view works without an internet connection. Unlike `plot()`, which computes its layout in Python
and draws a finished picture, `plot_vis()` hands the graph to a physics simulation that runs in the
browser. The nodes settle into place on screen and stay alive afterwards: dragging a node pulls its
neighbors along, and the network springs back into balance when it is let go.

The view takes its node colors from a `color` attribute stored on the nodes, which
[`colorize_node_attrs()`](../reference/Graph.colorize_node_attrs.qmd) prepares from a categorical
attribute (see [Aesthetics](aesthetics.qmd#visual-attributes-for-the-interactive-views)). For
the karate club, colored by faction:

```{python}
karate.colorize_node_attrs("faction", palette="Set2")
karate.plot_vis(width=640, height=480)
```

Each node is drawn as a circle holding its node ID, so the instructor is node 1 and the
administrator node 34. The label text adapts to the node color, white on dark colors and dark gray
on light ones. A few interactions are available:

- **dragging** a node moves it, and the simulation rearranges its neighbors around the new position
- **scrolling** zooms in and out around the pointer, and dragging the background pans the view
- the **Zoom Out**, **Reset View**, and **Zoom In** buttons below the canvas do the same with a
  smooth animation, and *Reset View* fits the whole graph into the canvas again
- **clicking** a node or an edge opens a panel in the top left corner listing its attributes, and
  clicking the background closes it

The click panel lists the stored attributes other than the visual ones, such as `faction`, `role`,
and `pagerank` here. Node labels are not part of it, so for graphs whose IDs mean little, it can
help to copy the labels into an ordinary attribute, such as `name`, before calling `plot_vis()`.
Edges are drawn as smooth curves, directed edges get arrowheads, and parallel edges between the same
two nodes are bent apart so that each one stays visible. An edge `color` attribute sets the color of
individual edges.

### Choosing where the view appears

`plot_vis()` writes the view to a self-contained HTML file in a temporary location, and then shows
it. With the default `target="auto"`, the view is displayed inline below the cell when the code
runs in a Jupyter or IPython session, and opened in the default web browser otherwise, such as from
a script or a terminal. `target="browser"` always opens a browser tab, which gives the view more
room than a notebook cell:

```{python}
#| eval: false
karate.plot_vis(target="browser", width=1200, height=800)
```

The method returns `None`, since the view is shown as a side effect. To write the HTML file to a
chosen path instead, for example to send it to a colleague or publish it on a website, use the
top-level function [`plot_graph()`](../reference/plot_graph.qmd), which takes the same options
together with `output_path=`, and returns the path of the file it wrote. With `open_browser=False`
and `display_inline=False`, it only writes the file:

```{python}
#| eval: false
ec.plot_graph(karate, output_path="karate-vis.html", open_browser=False, display_inline=False)
```

The file contains the vis-network library itself, about 700 KB, so it opens anywhere, offline as
well.

### Layout and static mode

With the default `layout="force"`, vis-network computes the positions itself. `layout="circular"`
and `layout="random"` give the simulation starting positions on a circle or at random instead, but
since the physics keeps running, the nodes then drift toward the same kind of balanced arrangement
as before. `static=True` stops the simulation once the initial layout has settled, and turns off
node dragging and hover effects, which keeps a chosen arrangement exactly as it is. A circle of
fixed nodes, in which every edge can be followed:

```{python}
#| eval: false
karate.plot_vis(layout="circular", static=True, edge_width=1)
```

`edge_width=` sets the width of every edge, and `width=` and `height=` the size of the canvas.

Since the simulation runs continuously in the browser, `plot_vis()` is at its best with up to a few
hundred nodes. For graphs of more than a thousand nodes, it settles the
layout in fewer steps, hides the edges while the view is dragged or zoomed, and turns off hover
effects to keep the view responsive, but `plot_cosmo()`, described below, is the better tool at that
scale.

## The graph widget

[`graph_widget()`](../reference/graph_widget.qmd) creates a `GraphWidget`, a lighter interactive
view drawn on an HTML canvas. It computes a force-directed layout in Python, and the browser then
draws the nodes and edges and handles the interaction: dragging a node moves it, dragging the
background pans, scrolling zooms around the pointer, and hovering over a node highlights it and
shows a tooltip with its ID and attributes. Unlike `plot_vis()`, the nodes don't move by
themselves once they are drawn.

The widget reads both of the stored visual attributes: `color` for the node color and `size` for
the node radius. Both can be prepared in advance with
[`colorize_node_attrs()`](../reference/Graph.colorize_node_attrs.qmd) and
[`rescale_node_attrs()`](../reference/Graph.rescale_node_attrs.qmd):

```{python}
karate.colorize_node_attrs("faction", palette="Set2")
karate.rescale_node_attrs("pagerank")
karate.get_node_df().select("id", "faction", "color", "pagerank", "size").head(4)
```

`rescale_node_attrs()` maps the PageRank scores onto its default range from 0.5 to 1. The widget
treats sizes between 0 and 1 as relative, and turns them into a radius of `node_size=` times
`0.5 + size × size_scale`, so with a `node_size=` of 8 the nodes here range from 8 to 12 pixels.
Sizes greater than 1 are taken as radii in pixels. The widget itself is created and displayed with
`show()`:

```{python}
#| eval: false
widget = ec.graph_widget(karate, width=600, height=450, node_size=8)
widget.show()
```

In a Jupyter notebook, `show()` displays the widget below the cell. It uses
[anywidget](https://anywidget.dev), which is installed along with EdgeCase. Outside a notebook,
or when anywidget is missing, `show()` falls back to `plot_vis()` in a browser
tab, which draws the graph with that view's own defaults rather than the widget's settings.

For a widget that works everywhere, `to_html()` writes a standalone HTML page with the same
interactive canvas, and returns its path:

```{python}
#| eval: false
widget.to_html("karate-widget.html")
```

### Mapping data in the widget

The widget can also derive colors and sizes from the data itself, much like `plot()`. `color_by=`
names a categorical attribute, with colors from one of the palettes `"default"`, `"vibrant"`,
`"pastel"`, `"dark"`, or `"tableau"`, chosen with `color_palette=`. `size_by=` names a numeric
attribute, which is scaled from half the base `node_size=` upward, with `size_scale=` setting how
far. Stored `color` and `size` attributes take precedence over both, so a graph that has been
through `colorize_node_attrs()` keeps its colors:

```{python}
#| eval: false
dolphins = ec.dolphins()
dolphins.cmty_louvain().degree_centrality()

ec.graph_widget(
    dolphins,
    color_by="cmty_louvain",
    color_palette="tableau",
    size_by="degree_centrality",
    size_scale=1.5,
    node_size=6,
).show()
```

The widget's palettes are its own, separate from the palettes of `plot()`, and the order in which
colors are assigned to the values may change between sessions. When the same colors must appear in
every view and every time, `colorize_node_attrs()` is the more reliable route, since it sorts the
values before assigning colors and stores the result on the graph.

The remaining options are `layout=`, which also accepts `"circular"` and `"random"`, `width=` and
`height=` for the canvas, `edge_width=`, and `background=` for the canvas color. The widget draws
every edge as a straight, undirected line, and draws a single line for a pair of nodes linked by
several edges, so for directed graphs and multigraphs `plot()` and `plot_vis()` are the better
choices.

## Large graphs with plot_cosmo()

`plot()`, `plot_vis()`, and the graph widget all slow down on graphs of a few thousand nodes.
`plot_cosmo()` hands the graph to [Cosmograph](https://cosmograph.app), which computes the layout
and draws the graph on the GPU with WebGL, and handles hundreds of thousands of nodes in the
browser. It needs the `cosmograph` package (`pip install cosmograph`) and runs as a Jupyter widget,
so it displays in a notebook rather than in a rendered document:

```{python}
#| eval: false
power_grid = ec.power_grid()
power_grid.cmty_louvain()
power_grid.plot_cosmo(point_color_by="cmty_louvain")
```

The layout of the 4,941 substations of the western United States power grid unfolds on screen as
the simulation runs on the GPU, with each community in its own color. The method passes the node
table and the edge table of the graph to Cosmograph, so its four mapping arguments name columns of
those tables:

- `point_color_by=` and `point_size_by=` name node attributes, such as a community or a centrality
  score
- `link_color_by=` and `link_width_by=` name edge attributes, including `"weight"`, which is a
  column of the edge table

All node and edge attributes are included in the hover and selection information, and the node
labels are used as point labels when the graph has them. Since the result is a `cosmograph`
widget, it can be configured further with the options of the Cosmograph library.

Even with GPU rendering, a drawing of a very large graph shows mostly its overall texture, such as
dense cores, long chains, and loosely attached periphery. The strategies of
[Static plots](plotting.qmd#larger-graphs), such as drawing a k-core or a single community, are
often the better way to see the detail.

## Step players

The last kind of interactive view replays a process rather than showing a finished graph. A *step
player* shows a sequence of frames with controls to step forward and back, play and pause, and
jump to any frame with a slider. Two families of methods produce them.

`plot_traversal()` and the recorder returned by `record_traversal()` animate a search through a
graph, lighting up nodes in the order they are reached, as described in
[Traversals](traversals.qmd#drawing-a-search):

```{python}
florentine = ec.florentine_families()
florentine.plot_traversal(source="Medici", algorithm="BFS")
```

The breadth-first search from the Medici reaches their six marriage partners first, then five
families two marriages away, and finally Bischeri, Peruzzi, and Lamberteschi, three steps out.

`play()` replays the graph's *step log*, the record of every operation that built or changed it, so
that each frame shows a step of the construction together with the code that performed it. It is
the subject of [The step log](step-log.qmd). Both kinds of player are `StepPlayer` objects, like
the result of `plot()`, so they display themselves in notebooks and rendered documents and can be
saved with `save()` to an HTML file that keeps all the controls.

## Summary

| Method | Displays | Colors and sizes from | Save with |
|---|---|---|---|
| `plot()` | inline, as SVG with tooltips | `color_by=`, `size_by=` | `output=` or `save()`, as `.svg` or `.html` |
| `plot_vis()` | inline in IPython, else in a browser | the stored `color` attribute | [`plot_graph(output_path=)`](../reference/plot_graph.qmd) |
| [`graph_widget()`](../reference/graph_widget.qmd) | `show()`, in a notebook | the stored `color` and `size` attributes, or `color_by=`, `size_by=` | `to_html()` |
| `plot_cosmo()` | as a Jupyter widget | `point_color_by=`, `point_size_by=`, `link_color_by=`, `link_width_by=` | the Cosmograph widget's own export |
| `plot_traversal()`, `play()` | inline, as a step player | the traversal or step log | `save()`, as `.html` |
